data.body:
Operator 2026-10-13: does it make sense for ddflow to implement ACP to communicate with and control agents; if so propose a phase and tasks.

Research note R-acp. Verdict: yes, as a client first, then the wrap proxy; no as an ACP agent; remote HTTP/WebSocket later. ACP is the lowest common denominator with the broadest reach (native in gemini, copilot (preview), kilo, cursor, kimi, opencode, qwen, devin, cline, goose, junie, augment, grok; adapters for claude, codex, amp, pi, glm; droid and antigravity have ACP modes; no ACP found for qodo, tabnine, aider, replit, cody, roo, continue, windsurf, vscode); native APIs beat it on fidelity for claude, codex and opencode, so ACP is a generic backend beside native ones, chosen per agent by a knob.
Reuse: the lane-backend interface, foreign ids and the ACP wrap task (P-control-planes: CP-backend-iface, CP-foreign-ids, CP-acp-wrap), the launcher, descriptors and continuation engine (P-agent-parity), spawn and notify (P-spawn), the approvals engine, capability envelope, event registry and evaluation harness (P-shared-engines, P-safeguards), the agent lifecycle verify (P-agent-lifecycle).
NEW: the ACP transport and v1 client, the registry reader, the update-to-event mapper, the permission broker, the turn loop, process lifecycle handling, steering, resume, the fake ACP agent and client fixtures, and the conformance run of the wrap proxy.
Rules: v1 only; advertise no fs or terminal capabilities; every permission request is decided by policy and logged; auth stays with the agent's own login; adapter versions are pinned from the registry and recorded; a missing or unauthenticated agent is unavailable, never passed; everything configurable, CLI+MCP+prompt, logged. Paced per D-usage-pacing-2026-10.

chunk_findings.detail: The record is stamped "status **accepted** · decided by operator", but its own text concedes that the operative part of the permission policy is not settled: "'the repo' means the repository the lane's worktree belongs to ... **Recorded reading, to be confirmed by the operator**". The intent for this task states the operator's recommendation was "allow inside the worktree, deny outside, ask otherwise" (i.e. worktree-only), while the answer actually recorded broadens the allow set to "AUTO-ALLOW everything inside the worktree AND THE REPO". Anyone implementing the downstream task AC-permissions reads only the accepted record and derives a policy that auto-allows every path anywhere in the repository (outside the worktree, outside the lane's scope), not just the worktree; the compensating exclusions (.git, .ddflow state, other lanes' worktrees) are listed only as a recorder's interpretation that has not been confirmed. The failure scenario: AC-permissions ships with the repo-wide auto-allow, and any tool call touching an ordinary source path elsewhere in the repository is approved without asking, contrary to what was recommended to the operator. Either the record should not be marked accepted while the reading is unconfirmed, or the confirmed scope must be written into the decision before it governs downstream tasks.

chunk_findings.detail: The record broadens auto-allow from the lane worktree to the whole repository and simultaneously drops the second half of the policy that was put to the operator ("allow inside the worktree, deny outside, ask otherwise"). Under this text a lane agent calling a tool on `<repo>/scripts/deploy.sh` — a tracked file in the shared main checkout, not in the lane's worktree — is auto-allowed, because the never-auto-allowed list covers only `.git`, ddflow's `.ddflow` state/event shards and other lanes' worktrees, and nothing in main's working tree is excluded. That means an agent can mutate files that concurrent work and the acceptance flow (D-push-after-acceptance) depend on without any prompt, which is exactly the isolation the worktree model exists to provide; and no rule at all is stated for paths outside the repo, so the "deny outside / ask otherwise" half has no recorded default for AC-permissions to implement.

Reuses the capability envelope and path scope (P-safeguards.envelope) and approvals (SE-ask-core); a too-wide auto-allow is the main security risk, so the default is narrow and the policy is a record kind with history.

(4) permission policy: allow inside the worktree, deny outside, ask otherwise, always logged; rec: yes. (5) steering by capability: native extension where present, else cancel plus prompt; rec: yes. chunk_findings.detail: The record is stamped "status **accepted** · decided by operator", but its own text concedes that the operative part of the permission policy is not settled: "'the repo' means the repository the lane's worktree belongs to ... **Recorded reading, to be confirmed by the operator**". The intent for this task states the operator's recommendation was "allow inside the worktree, deny outside, ask otherwise" (i.e. worktree-only), while the answer actually recorded broadens the allow set to "AUTO-ALLOW everything inside the worktree AND THE REPO". Anyone implementing the downstream task AC-permissions reads only the accepted record and derives a policy that auto-allows every path anywhere in the repository (outside the worktree, outside the lane's scope), not just the worktree; the compensating exclusions (.git, .ddflow state, other lanes' worktrees) are listed only as a recorder's interpretation that has not been confirmed. The failure scenario: AC-permissions ships with the repo-wide auto-allow, and any tool call touching an ordinary source path elsewhere in the repository is approved without asking, contrary to what was recommended to the operator. Either the record should not be marked accepted while the reading is unconfirmed, or the confirmed scope must be written into the decision before it governs downstream tasks.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/acp.md:8

chunk_findings.detail: The record broadens auto-allow from the lane worktree to the whole repository and simultaneously drops the second half of the policy that was put to the operator ("allow inside the worktree, deny outside, ask otherwise"). Under this text a lane agent calling a tool on `<repo>/scripts/deploy.sh` — a tracked file in the shared main checkout, not in the lane's worktree — is auto-allowed, because the never-auto-allowed list covers only `.git`, ddflow's `.ddflow` state/event shards and other lanes' worktrees, and nothing in main's working tree is excluded. That means an agent can mutate files that concurrent work and the acceptance flow (D-push-after-acceptance) depend on without any prompt, which is exactly the isolation the worktree model exists to provide; and no rule at all is stated for paths outside the repo, so the "deny outside / ask otherwise" half has no recorded default for AC-permissions to implement.

chunk_findings.detail: The document is committed as the decision of record, but the sentence that carries the entire change from the recommendation ("the repo" meaning the whole parent repository) is an interpretation the document itself marks as unconfirmed. A reader — `ddflow decision show D-acp`, a hook, or the AC-permissions/AC-eval tasks named in the Consequences — sees `accepted` and takes the repo-wide auto-allow as ratified operator intent, since the record is declared the source of truth; the unratified reading then becomes the shipped default. Either the confirmation happened and the hedge should not be in the accepted record, or it did not and the record must not assert accepted status for that clause.

It is about 3,000 words. Every claim has a source URL and is tagged [FETCHED], [SNIPPET], [UNVERIFIED] or [INFERENCE]. I did not read ddflow's code. The ddflow recommendations rest only on the context in your brief.

## Key findings

- **What Copilot's tiers do:**
  - Efficiency, Balance and Intelligence share one model pool and change only how Auto prefers models. Auto still judges each prompt, and you are billed for the model it picks. Paid plans get a 10% discount. Source: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-14-configure-cost-and-quality-in-copilot-auto-model-selection
  - Auto switches models only at natural cache boundaries: the first turn and after compaction. Source: https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/getting-more-from-each-token-how-copilot-improves-context-handling-and-model-routing/
  - That boundary rule explains the cache-reset notice.
- **Cache cost of switching in Claude Code:**
  - Each model has its own cache, so `/model` forces a full uncached re-read. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching
  - A top-level effort change also resets the cache on most models, but not on the 5.5-class models.
  - Per-message effort in the API keeps the cache.
  - Toggling the advisor tool keeps the cache. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/advisor
  - Cache reads cost about 0.1x input, 5-minute writes 1.25x, and 1-hour writes 2x. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
- **Research on coding-agent routing:**
  - The most relevant work is SWE-Router, Agent-as-a-Router and Triage. SWE-Router runs a cheap model for 3 turns and then decides whether to escalate. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00053
  - Trajectory-based routing beat prompt-only routing by about 15 percentage points. RouteLLM and FrugalGPT are single-shot results and should not be assumed to transfer to long agent loops.
- **Programmatic control per harness:**
  - Copilot CLI's ACP server fixes reasoning effort at launch, and `session/new` carries no model or effort. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/acp-server
  - The ACP protocol itself does define session config option categories for model and thought level. Source: https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/session-config-options

## Top 3 of the ranked 10 for the governor

1. **Cache-aware switching.** Switch tier only at safe points, with a switch-cost estimate.
2. **Per-agent capability table.** Record which routing doors each harness has, and whether each preserves the cache.
3. **`optimize_for` preset.** An efficiency/balance/intelligence setting that compiles to the existing ladder knobs and cannot override guardrail floors.

The remaining seven cover routing by stage and role, escalation on gate failures, review findings and loops, guardrail floors, recording the model that actually ran, regret and yield reports, hysteresis, and replay/A-B evaluation. The report also has ten concrete task ideas.

## What I could not verify

- **Notice text:** I did not find the exact "resets the prompt cache" string on any page, though the behaviour is consistent with the cache-boundary design.
- **Effort and settings:** Whether a tier changes reasoning effort, and any VS Code setting keys for the tier, are also unverified.
- **Blocked or thin sources:** The Visual Studio Magazine hands-on article returned a 403. Cursor's own docs returned only a generic summary, so the Cursor router details come from a third-party blog. Windsurf, Augment and Devin specifics were not reliably sourced.

data.claim: Copilot's three settings share one model pool and only change how Auto prefers models; Auto switches only at natural cache boundaries (the first turn and after compaction), which is why a mid-session change warns about the prompt-cache reset. Each model has its own cache (cache reads about 0.1x input, writes 1.25x to 2x), so a model switch pays a full uncached re-read; a top-level effort change can also reset the cache, per-message effort and an advisor model do not. Routing evidence for agents is thin and recent (SWE-Router, Agent-as-a-Router, Triage): trajectory-based routing beat prompt-only routing by about 15 points; single-shot results (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT) should not be assumed to transfer to long loops. So ddflow should add: switching only at safe points with an estimated switch cost, a per-agent routing capability table, an optimize_for preset compiled into the existing ladder knobs, role and stage routing (planner, implementer, reviewer, triage), cascade-with-escalation on ddflow's own signals (gate failures, loops, reviewer rejection, context ladder), guardrails presets cannot lower, step-cost events that record the model that actually ran, a regret and yield report with a per-tier break-even, and replay and A/B evaluation.
data.falsifier: If a seeded replay shows the preset or escalation policy lowering a reviewer below its floor, switching mid-lane without a cost estimate, oscillating between tiers, or costing more per merged task than always-balanced, the design is wrong.
data.mechanism: The governor's decision function and ladders stay; a preset layer compiles to knobs; a capability table (extending the descriptor facts and ACP session config options) says which door switches model or effort and whether it preserves the cache; the escalation policy consumes gate, loop and review signals and emits requests applied at safe points; step-cost events feed the spend ledger and the regret report; replay of the event log scores policies.

chunk_findings.detail:
`is_stale()` treats any failure to read the tree as "the process is current": the entire scan, including `p.stat()`, sits inside `try: ... except OSError: return False`. The safe answer when the tree cannot be read is "assume stale" (or propagate the error so it becomes a `FreshError`/`ManifestError`); returning `False` selects the *unsafe* branch and makes `running_code()` fall back to the process's stale `knob_defaults()`/`event_kinds()`, which is precisely the state this change exists to avoid.

Concretely: `root.rglob("*.py")` yields paths by directory traversal and `p.stat()` is evaluated lazily inside `any(...)`. If a file disappears between being yielded and being stat'd — e.g. an in-place upgrade replacing/removing package files, which is exactly the moment `is_stale()` is meant to run in — `p.stat()` raises `FileNotFoundError`; that escapes `any()`, is caught by `except OSError`, and `is_stale()` returns `False`. The same happens for a dangling `*.py` symlink or a transient I/O error on a network-mounted package dir. Then `running_code()` (upgrade_manifest.py ~line 307) returns `knob_defaults(), event_kinds()` from the long-lived process instead of `UR.fresh()`, and `lint()` again reports the phantom `knob_removed` changes and refuses `ddflow version cut` for changes that do not exist — the exact failure B72b73360bc describes, still reachable through an unreadable/broken/racing source file.

chunk_findings.detail: The only functional change in this diff is the OSError branch of `is_stale()`. The reported repro is not an unreadable-tree case: a fresh CLI process reads the same tree and prints "release manifest lint (block): 0 unmanifested", so `Path(...).rglob("*.py")` does not raise in that environment. Therefore this branch is never taken for the input that matters — a long-lived MCP server whose `upgrade_manifest.knob_defaults()` was built at import, with the knob source files newer than the server start but fully readable. Given that input, `is_stale()` already returns a result based on `p.stat().st_mtime > _STARTED` (or the lint never consults it), and the stale import-time registry is still what the lint compares against the manifest; the 11 phantom `knob_removed` changes (importer.phase_slug_chars, lanes.advise_max, log.commit_events_at, …) are still reported and `ddflow_version_cut` still refuses. The fix direction in the intent — rebuild the registry per call or read the knob defaults from disk instead of caching them in the long-lived process — is not implemented anywhere in this diff; nothing removes or invalidates the cached `knob_defaults()`.

chunk_findings.detail: `is_stale()` decides “the tree on disk has moved on” purely by comparing `.py` mtimes against `_STARTED = time.time()` captured at import of `upgrade_registry`. Mtime is not a property of *content*, and many real ways of getting new code onto disk preserve or backdate it: `tar -x`, `rsync -a`/`cp -p`, and extraction of a wheel (pip writes each file with the timestamp recorded in the zip entry, i.e. the build time, not the install time). Concrete failure: the MCP server starts at T0 and imports `ddflow.services.upgrade_manifest` (so the in-memory knob registry is built at T0); at T1 the package is updated/redeployed with mtimes preserved from an earlier build (say T-1), which adds exactly the knobs from the bug report (`lanes.advise_max`, `log.commit_events_at`, …). At T2 a `ddflow version lint`/`version cut` runs in that same server: `is_stale()` scans `ddflow/*.py`, finds every `st_mtime <= _STARTED`, returns `False`, `running_code()` therefore falls through to the stale `knob_defaults()`/`event_kinds()`, and the manifest on disk (read fresh, so it announces the new knobs) again reports them as `knob_removed` and refuses the release. That is precisely B72b73360bc, and it violates the stated fix direction that “a stale process must not be able to refuse a release for changes that do not exist.” The check needs a signal that tracks content/identity of the source (e.g. hash of the registry modules, or comparing the manifest/registry version against the code), not wall-clock mtimes; alternatively the fresh subprocess must be consulted unconditionally for lint purposes so that the stale process’s cached registry can never drive the comparison.

chunk_findings.detail: The whole fix hinges on `is_stale()` deciding "this process runs older code than the tree" from the test `p.stat().st_mtime > _STARTED`, i.e. from the *file mtime* of a `.py` under the package being later than the module's import time. A `.py` mtime is not a reliable proxy for "the code under this process changed": many ways of moving the tree forward leave mtimes at or below the old process's start time. `pip`/`uv` installing a wheel extract the archive members with the timestamp recorded in the wheel (the build time, not the install time); `tar -x` and `cp -p` restores preserve timestamps; coarse-grained or clock-skewed filesystems can also leave `st_mtime <= _STARTED`. In any of those cases `is_stale()` returns False, `running_code()` falls back to `knob_defaults(), event_kinds()` of the long-lived process, and the exact bug B72b73360bc remains: given an MCP server started at 12:00 and an upgrade at 12:30 to a wheel of release 0.2.2 that was built at 09:00, the installed `ddflow/**.py` keep their 09:00 mtimes, so no file is newer than `_STARTED`; `version lint`/`cut` then compares the stale in-memory registry with the freshly read 0.2.2 manifest and again reports the 11 knobs added since server start (`importer.phase_slug_chars`, `lanes.advise_max`, `log.commit_events_at`, …) as `knob_removed`, refusing the cut, while a fresh CLI in the same tree prints "0 unmanifested, 0 waived". Since the mtime probe is the only gate that selects the fresh-registry path, the fix silently no-ops precisely in the long-lived-server upgrade scenarios it was written for.

data.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_registry.py: is_stale / _STARTED

chunk_findings.detail: The whole fix hinges on `is_stale()` deciding "this process runs older code than the tree" from the test `p.stat().st_mtime > _STARTED`, i.e. from the *file mtime* of a `.py` under the package being later than the module's import time. A `.py` mtime is not a reliable proxy for "the code under this process changed": many ways of moving the tree forward leave mtimes at or below the old process's start time. `pip`/`uv` installing a wheel extract the archive members with the timestamp recorded in the wheel (the build time, not the install time); `tar -x` and `cp -p` restores preserve timestamps; coarse-grained or clock-skewed filesystems can also leave `st_mtime <= _STARTED`. In any of those cases `is_stale()` returns False, `running_code()` falls back to `knob_defaults(), event_kinds()` of the long-lived process, and the exact bug B72b73360bc remains: given an MCP server started at 12:00 and an upgrade at 12:30 to a wheel of release 0.2.2 that was built at 09:00, the installed `ddflow/**.py` keep their 09:00 mtimes, so no file is newer than `_STARTED`; `version lint`/`cut` then compares the stale in-memory registry with the freshly read 0.2.2 manifest and again reports the 11 knobs added since server start (`importer.phase_slug_chars`, `lanes.advise_max`, `log.commit_events_at`, …) as `knob_removed`, refusing the cut, while a fresh CLI in the same tree prints "0 unmanifested, 0 waived". Since the mtime probe is the only gate that selects the fresh-registry path, the fix silently no-ops precisely in the long-lived-server upgrade scenarios it was written for.

data.summary: `ddflow abandon` (api/lifecycle/complete.abandon) only appends item.abandoned and releases the lease; `remove` only appends task.removed and releases. Neither disposes the item's worktree or its ddflow/<id> branch, unlike `merge`, whose dispose_tree removes a clean tree and deletes the merged branch with `git branch -d`. So an abandoned or removed item keeps its tree and branch indefinitely, and the doctor reports it as an orphan worktree. Repro 2026-10-14: B-docs-config was abandoned and its worktree stayed until removed by hand (its 2 unmerged commits were meant to be kept, but nothing recorded or distinguished that). Fix direction: on abandon or remove, run dispose_tree for a clean tree with no unmerged commits (tree and branch go); a tree that holds uncommitted files or unmerged commits is KEPT, the outcome says so and names the branch and the command to inspect it, and an explicit flag (for example --discard) drops it after writing a backup ref; adopted and borrowed trees are never touched. Regression tests: abandon of an item with a clean merged tree removes tree and branch; with unmerged commits keeps both and says so.

chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the removal event *before* it evaluates `_dispose`, and `_dispose` does not receive the already-computed `it` — it re-reads the log and looks the item up again:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", id=item, children=[], dependents=[],
            **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd)))
```

`remove`'s own docstring/behaviour is "take an item out of the queue entirely", i.e. after `task.removed`/`phase.removed` the item is no longer present in the folded state. So inside `_dispose` the `it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)` lookup yields `None`, and the `if it is not None else (False, "")` branch returns `worktree_removed=False, kept_reason=""`. Concretely: run `ddflow remove <id>` on an item whose worktree is clean and fully merged — the outcome reports `"worktree_removed": false` with an empty `kept_reason`, `CL.dispose_finished` is never called, and both the worktree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch remain on disk, so the doctor still flags the orphan worktree. This is exactly the failure the change claims to fix, and it survives because the item's absence is silently swallowed instead of disposing based on the state captured before the append (the same `it` the function already holds and uses for `it.kind`/`it.lease`). Note the intent's regression list only covers `abandon` ("abandon of an item with a clean merged tree removes tree and branch"), so this path is the one the planned tests would not exercise.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:370 (`remove` → `_dispose`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob defaults to `True` and its own doc states it removes a finished item's worktree and branch on `complete`, `abandon` and `remove` (and sweeps DONE items at `brief`), yet the existing `worktree.remove_on_merge` knob is the documented way to keep a merged tree for post-mortem inspection ("Disable while debugging the pipeline so post-mortem inspection is possible"). A project that already has `worktree.remove_on_merge = false` and upgrades gets `dispose_finished = true` for free, so running `ddflow complete <item>` on a clean, fully-merged tree now runs the new dispose step and deletes the tree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch — exactly the setting the operator had turned off. The doc's escape clause ("Turn off to keep every tree for post-mortems, the way `remove_on_merge = false` does for a merge") only works if the operator knows to set the *new* knob; the old explicit opt-out is silently overridden on the `complete`/`brief` paths. Concrete input: existing config `worktree.remove_on_merge = false`, run `ddflow complete <clean merged item>` — merge keeps the tree via `_dispose`'s `remove_on_merge` guard, then the complete-level `dispose_finished` step removes it anyway. If instead the complete path really does go through `_dispose` (guarded by `remove_on_merge`), then the new knob's doc is wrong to claim it governs `complete` at all; either branch of that fork is a defect in the added config surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/worktree.py:43 (`worktree.dispose_finished`)

chunk_findings.detail: The branch is only ever deleted through `dispose_tree`, but that call is skipped whenever the recorded worktree directory is missing. Input: an item whose tree directory has already been removed by hand (`git worktree remove --force`, `rm -rf`, or a previous failed run — the intent's own repro says "its worktree stayed until removed by hand"), while the branch `ddflow/<id>` still exists. `W.load_path(repo, it.worktree)` returns the (now nonexistent) path, `path.exists()` is False, the function returns `(False, "")`, and `dispose_tree` — the only place that runs `git branch -d` — never runs. So `ddflow abandon`/`ddflow remove` still leave the branch behind indefinitely and report nothing at all, which is exactly the defect B79319c6ada describes (tree + branch left behind; doctor still flags the orphan). The clean-tree-with-no-unmerged-commits case is the common one, so this is not an exotic corner.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:dispose_finished (`if not path.exists(): return False, ""`)

chunk_findings.detail: `dispose_finished` deliberately computes a second element in the removed case — `return True, (f"branch {it.branch} left: {gone.branch_left}" if gone.branch_left else "")` — i.e. the branch survived (dispose_tree removed a clean tree but could not delete the branch, e.g. it is still checked out elsewhere or `git branch -d` refused against the configured base). Input: a DONE item older than `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` in that state. `sweep_finished` only reports `f"removed the finished worktree of {it.id}"` and throws the second element away whenever `removed` is truthy, so the operator is never told that `ddflow/<id>` was left behind and how to inspect it — contradicting the stated requirement that a kept branch is named in the outcome.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:sweep_finished (`if removed: out.append(...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `call_kwargs=L.merge_kwargs` to abandon/remove/complete, but the new `call` lambdas accept only `called_from` and `shell_cwd`, and they forward only `reason`/`force` (plus `called_from`/`shell_cwd`) to `_api().abandon` and `_api().remove_item`. No `discard` parameter exists in either lambda, and no `discard` Param is added to the `params` tuple. The stated fix promises “an explicit flag (for example --discard) drops it after writing a backup ref”, but with this surface there is no path for such a flag to reach the API: running `ddflow abandon <id> --discard` either forwards a keyword the lambda does not declare (because `L.merge_kwargs` is supplied as call kwargs) and raises `TypeError`, or silently ignores the flag if the framework filters it, leaving the worktree and branch in place. Either way the regression case for the explicit-discard path cannot pass, and the intended disposal after the flag never occurs. The same merge-kwargs reuse on `complete` applies merge options to a command whose lambda does not accept them.

chunk_findings.detail: `sweep_finished` calls `dispose_finished(repo, cfg, log, it)` without the `callers` argument, even though `dispose_finished` exists precisely to avoid removing a tree the caller is standing in (`stands_in`, the B1172da8c35 guard), and `sweep_finished` is the caller most likely to run inside such a tree (it is described as running at "session start", i.e. in the user's/agent's shell process). The only guard it has left is `worktree.sweep_min_age_s`, and age does not tell you where the current process's cwd is: an agent that starts a session in the leftover worktree of an item that was finished (merged) earlier than `sweep_min_age_s` — a normal resumption/inspection case, and exactly the "merge keeps the tree it was run from" case the sweep is aimed at — gets the tree deleted under it. Given a DONE item B-x with a clean worktree at `[REDACTED:path]`, `completed_at` older than `sweep_min_age_s`, and `cwd = [REDACTED:path]` (or a subdirectory), `sweep_finished` iterates it, skips the age check, and calls `dispose_finished` with `callers == ()`; `stands_in` is never consulted, `dispose_tree` removes the directory, and the shell is left in a deleted directory — the B1172da8c35 failure the new helper was written to prevent. Passing `callers=(Path.cwd(),)` (or the equivalent for the invoking shell) here would close it; the other callers of `dispose_finished` can pass their cwd but this one cannot, since it receives none.

chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the removal event *before* it evaluates `_dispose`, and `_dispose` does not receive the already-computed `it` — it re-reads the log and looks the item up again:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", id=item, children=[], dependents=[],
            **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd)))
```

`remove`'s own docstring/behaviour is "take an item out of the queue entirely", i.e. after `task.removed`/`phase.removed` the item is no longer present in the folded state. So inside `_dispose` the `it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)` lookup yields `None`, and the `if it is not None else (False, "")` branch returns `worktree_removed=False, kept_reason=""`. Concretely: run `ddflow remove <id>` on an item whose worktree is clean and fully merged — the outcome reports `"worktree_removed": false` with an empty `kept_reason`, `CL.dispose_finished` is never called, and both the worktree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch remain on disk, so the doctor still flags the orphan worktree. This is exactly the failure the change claims to fix, and it survives because the item's absence is silently swallowed instead of disposing based on the state captured before the append (the same `it` the function already holds and uses for `it.kind`/`it.lease`). Note the intent's regression list only covers `abandon` ("abandon of an item with a clean merged tree removes tree and branch"), so this path is the one the planned tests would not exercise.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:370 (`remove` → `_dispose`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob defaults to `True` and its own doc states it removes a finished item's worktree and branch on `complete`, `abandon` and `remove` (and sweeps DONE items at `brief`), yet the existing `worktree.remove_on_merge` knob is the documented way to keep a merged tree for post-mortem inspection ("Disable while debugging the pipeline so post-mortem inspection is possible"). A project that already has `worktree.remove_on_merge = false` and upgrades gets `dispose_finished = true` for free, so running `ddflow complete <item>` on a clean, fully-merged tree now runs the new dispose step and deletes the tree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch — exactly the setting the operator had turned off. The doc's escape clause ("Turn off to keep every tree for post-mortems, the way `remove_on_merge = false` does for a merge") only works if the operator knows to set the *new* knob; the old explicit opt-out is silently overridden on the `complete`/`brief` paths. Concrete input: existing config `worktree.remove_on_merge = false`, run `ddflow complete <clean merged item>` — merge keeps the tree via `_dispose`'s `remove_on_merge` guard, then the complete-level `dispose_finished` step removes it anyway. If instead the complete path really does go through `_dispose` (guarded by `remove_on_merge`), then the new knob's doc is wrong to claim it governs `complete` at all; either branch of that fork is a defect in the added config surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/worktree.py:43 (`worktree.dispose_finished`)

chunk_findings.detail: The branch is only ever deleted through `dispose_tree`, but that call is skipped whenever the recorded worktree directory is missing. Input: an item whose tree directory has already been removed by hand (`git worktree remove --force`, `rm -rf`, or a previous failed run — the intent's own repro says "its worktree stayed until removed by hand"), while the branch `ddflow/<id>` still exists. `W.load_path(repo, it.worktree)` returns the (now nonexistent) path, `path.exists()` is False, the function returns `(False, "")`, and `dispose_tree` — the only place that runs `git branch -d` — never runs. So `ddflow abandon`/`ddflow remove` still leave the branch behind indefinitely and report nothing at all, which is exactly the defect B79319c6ada describes (tree + branch left behind; doctor still flags the orphan). The clean-tree-with-no-unmerged-commits case is the common one, so this is not an exotic corner.

chunk_findings.detail: `brief` is the entry point for every session start, and it now unconditionally invokes `CL.sweep_finished`, whose stated criterion is only "DONE items finished long enough ago" (`worktree.dispose_finished` defaults to `true`, `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` to `3600`). That criterion is not the one the fix direction for this change mandates: disposal is only allowed for a *clean* tree with *no unmerged commits*, and "adopted and borrowed trees are never touched", with any kept tree reported by naming its branch and the command to inspect it. Nothing in the calling code enforces any of that, and the helper discards the call's result entirely (it returns `None`), so no kept/removed outcome is ever surfaced to the operator. Concretely: an item created with the default `worktree.adopt_existing = true` (a pre-existing directory the user adopted) that reaches DONE and is left alone for an hour is removed by the next `brief` run from *any* agent — including a `brief` issued from inside that very worktree by a session that is still using it (the process' CWD becomes a deleted directory, and its relative paths fail). The same happens to a DONE-but-not-yet-merged item whose only tree is clean but whose branch has unmerged commits, if the sweep's own cleanliness/merge check is missing or weaker than the one required for `abandon`/`remove`. Because `_sweep_finished` wraps the call in `except Exception: pass`, none of this is reported: if the sweep is wrong or only partially completes (tree gone, git metadata left behind), the operator sees no error and the doctor's orphan report quietly persists or changes shape. The unsafe part is the silent, default-on destructive side effect in a session-start read path with no operator-visible outcome; the testable input is "worktree adopted (or DONE with unmerged commits), age > `worktree.sweep_min_age_s`, then any `ddflow brief`".

chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the node-deletion event *before* delegating to `_dispose`, and `_dispose` re-derives the item from a fresh fold:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", ..., **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd)))
...
it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)
removed, why = CL.dispose_finished(repo, cfg, log, it, callers=callers) if it is not None else (False, "")
```

The removal event is deliberately node-scoped (`task.removed` / `phase.removed` — "Take an item out of the queue entirely"), unlike `item.abandoned`, which is a state transition that keeps the node. Once that event is in the log, the re-fold no longer yields the item, so `it is None`, the `if it is not None` guard short-circuits, and `dispose_finished` is never invoked for `remove`. Concretely: `ddflow remove <id>` on an item with a clean merged worktree leaves `[REDACTED:path]<id>` and `ddflow/<id>` in place exactly as before the fix, and the outcome it prints is `worktree_removed: false` with `kept_reason: ""` — i.e. no disposal and no explanation, so the operator cannot even tell that the tree was kept. This is the same bug B79319c6ada for the `remove` half; because `_dispose` swallows the missing-item case as `(False, "")` instead of an error or the real reason, it also cannot be noticed from the output. (The stated regression tests only cover `abandon`, which is why this path is not caught.) Moving the `_dispose` call above the terminal `log.append`, or passing the already-folded `it` in, would fix the ordering.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py (remove, `**_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd))`)

chunk_findings.detail: `dispose_finished` only protects a live shell via the explicit `callers` tuple (`stands_in(path, *callers)`), and `sweep_finished` invokes it as `dispose_finished(repo, cfg, log, it)` with the default `callers=()`. `stands_in` then iterates over an empty sequence and always returns `False`, so the guard that exists precisely to avoid "the next `pwd` fails" (B1172da8c35, quoted in the new `stands_in` docstring) is inert on the session-start sweep. Given a DONE item whose tree was kept at merge time because its caller stood in it, a shell that stays in that worktree past `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` and then runs the session-start sweep gets its cwd deleted: the age gate only proves the item finished long ago, not that anyone left the directory. `sweep_finished` should pass the process'/client's cwd the same way the `merge` path does.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py — `sweep_finished` calls `dispose_finished` without `callers`

chunk_findings.detail: When `stands_in` keeps a tree, `dispose_finished` returns the sentence "...cd <repo root> -- the next `ddflow brief` or `ddflow cleanup --apply` removes it." `dispose_finished` is the routine abandon and remove call, and the only `brief`-time mechanism added here is `sweep_finished`, which does `if it.removed or it.state != DONE ...: continue` — it only ever revisits `DONE` items. An abandoned item (state `ABANDONED`) or a removed item (`it.removed`) whose tree was kept because the caller stood in it therefore has no `brief`-time path that removes it, so it keeps its worktree and branch indefinitely — exactly the leftover the change is supposed to eliminate, and the reason the abandon outcome is allowed to keep the tree. Either the sweep must cover abandoned/removed items or the message must stop promising `ddflow brief`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the terminal event *before* building its outcome:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", id=item, children=[], dependents=[], **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, ...))
```

`_dispose` does not receive the `it` that `remove` already folded at the top of the function; it re-folds the whole log itself (`it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)`) and then, crucially, swallows the "item not found" case: `(False, "")` if `it is None`. Because `task.removed`/`phase.removed` is the event that takes the item out of the queue (the function's own docstring: "Take an item out of the queue entirely", and the outcome is `item.removed` with `children=[]`/`dependents=[]`), the fresh fold performed inside `_dispose` no longer contains the item. The guard therefore fires, `_dispose` returns `{"worktree_removed": False, "kept_reason": ""}`, and `remove` silently reports that nothing was disposed — the worktree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch are left exactly as before. Demonstrated input: `ddflow remove <id>` on an item with a clean, fully-merged worktree — the outcome carries `worktree_removed: false` and `kept_reason: ""`, the `ddflow/<id>` branch still exists, and the doctor still lists the tree as an orphan worktree, i.e. bug B79319c6ada is unfixed on the `remove` path. `abandon` does not hit this only because `item.abandoned` leaves the item present in the fold (the model keeps ABANDONED items); `remove` needs `_dispose` to be fed the already-folded item (or to run before the removal event is appended).

chunk_findings.detail: The fix direction this change is implementing states that "adopted and borrowed trees are never touched". Both new entry points only test the item-level `adopted` flag: `dispose_finished` guards with `if not it.worktree or it.adopted: return False, ""` and `sweep_finished` filters with `... or it.adopted or it.lease`. There is no borrowed case anywhere in the added code, and `dispose_finished` does not pass the item's real worktree record down to the disposer — it fabricates a bare `W.Worktree(item=it.id, path=path, branch=it.branch, base=base)` from three scalars, so any provenance the real worktree record carries (the thing that distinguishes "this tree belongs to another item / was borrowed") is dropped before `dispose_tree` sees it. Concretely: item B whose worktree is borrowed from another item (clean, committed, merged into base, no live lease — exactly the state `dispose_finished` treats as disposable) is the input; on `ddflow abandon B`/`remove B`, or at the next session-start `sweep_finished` once `it.completed_at` is older than `worktree.sweep_min_age_s`, `gone.removed` is true and the *lender's* worktree directory and its `ddflow/<id>` branch are removed — `_drop_branch` will even delete the branch when the tree is already gone, since it likewise only consults `_protected`/leases, never a borrowed marker. The regression tests named in the intent (clean merged tree vs unmerged commits) cannot catch this, because both scenarios use an item-owned tree; a borrowed tree is precisely the case the guard is supposed to cover and the code has no guard for it.

chunk_findings.detail: The change is presented as the fix for B79319c6ada — `ddflow abandon` / `ddflow remove` leaving the item's worktree and `ddflow/<id>` branch behind — but the entire diff is a new test module for a different defect, named in its own docstring as B4757c428f4 ("a merged item's worktree is kept when merge runs inside it; later commands remove it"). chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the removal event *before* it evaluates `_dispose`, and `_dispose` does not receive the already-computed `it` — it re-reads the log and looks the item up again:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", id=item, children=[], dependents=[],
            **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd)))
```

`remove`'s own docstring/behaviour is "take an item out of the queue entirely", i.e. after `task.removed`/`phase.removed` the item is no longer present in the folded state. So inside `_dispose` the `it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)` lookup yields `None`, and the `if it is not None else (False, "")` branch returns `worktree_removed=False, kept_reason=""`. Concretely: run `ddflow remove <id>` on an item whose worktree is clean and fully merged — the outcome reports `"worktree_removed": false` with an empty `kept_reason`, `CL.dispose_finished` is never called, and both the worktree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch remain on disk, so the doctor still flags the orphan worktree. This is exactly the failure the change claims to fix, and it survives because the item's absence is silently swallowed instead of disposing based on the state captured before the append (the same `it` the function already holds and uses for `it.kind`/`it.lease`). Note the intent's regression list only covers `abandon` ("abandon of an item with a clean merged tree removes tree and branch"), so this path is the one the planned tests would not exercise.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:370 (`remove` → `_dispose`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob defaults to `True` and its own doc states it removes a finished item's worktree and branch on `complete`, `abandon` and `remove` (and sweeps DONE items at `brief`), yet the existing `worktree.remove_on_merge` knob is the documented way to keep a merged tree for post-mortem inspection ("Disable while debugging the pipeline so post-mortem inspection is possible"). A project that already has `worktree.remove_on_merge = false` and upgrades gets `dispose_finished = true` for free, so running `ddflow complete <item>` on a clean, fully-merged tree now runs the new dispose step and deletes the tree and the `ddflow/<id>` branch — exactly the setting the operator had turned off. The doc's escape clause ("Turn off to keep every tree for post-mortems, the way `remove_on_merge = false` does for a merge") only works if the operator knows to set the *new* knob; the old explicit opt-out is silently overridden on the `complete`/`brief` paths. Concrete input: existing config `worktree.remove_on_merge = false`, run `ddflow complete <clean merged item>` — merge keeps the tree via `_dispose`'s `remove_on_merge` guard, then the complete-level `dispose_finished` step removes it anyway. If instead the complete path really does go through `_dispose` (guarded by `remove_on_merge`), then the new knob's doc is wrong to claim it governs `complete` at all; either branch of that fork is a defect in the added config surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/worktree.py:43 (`worktree.dispose_finished`)

chunk_findings.detail: The branch is only ever deleted through `dispose_tree`, but that call is skipped whenever the recorded worktree directory is missing. Input: an item whose tree directory has already been removed by hand (`git worktree remove --force`, `rm -rf`, or a previous failed run — the intent's own repro says "its worktree stayed until removed by hand"), while the branch `ddflow/<id>` still exists. `W.load_path(repo, it.worktree)` returns the (now nonexistent) path, `path.exists()` is False, the function returns `(False, "")`, and `dispose_tree` — the only place that runs `git branch -d` — never runs. So `ddflow abandon`/`ddflow remove` still leave the branch behind indefinitely and report nothing at all, which is exactly the defect B79319c6ada describes (tree + branch left behind; doctor still flags the orphan). The clean-tree-with-no-unmerged-commits case is the common one, so this is not an exotic corner.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:dispose_finished (`if not path.exists(): return False, ""`)

chunk_findings.detail: `dispose_finished` deliberately computes a second element in the removed case — `return True, (f"branch {it.branch} left: {gone.branch_left}" if gone.branch_left else "")` — i.e. the branch survived (dispose_tree removed a clean tree but could not delete the branch, e.g. it is still checked out elsewhere or `git branch -d` refused against the configured base). Input: a DONE item older than `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` in that state. `sweep_finished` only reports `f"removed the finished worktree of {it.id}"` and throws the second element away whenever `removed` is truthy, so the operator is never told that `ddflow/<id>` was left behind and how to inspect it — contradicting the stated requirement that a kept branch is named in the outcome.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:sweep_finished (`if removed: out.append(...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `call_kwargs=L.merge_kwargs` to abandon/remove/complete, but the new `call` lambdas accept only `called_from` and `shell_cwd`, and they forward only `reason`/`force` (plus `called_from`/`shell_cwd`) to `_api().abandon` and `_api().remove_item`. No `discard` parameter exists in either lambda, and no `discard` Param is added to the `params` tuple. The stated fix promises “an explicit flag (for example --discard) drops it after writing a backup ref”, but with this surface there is no path for such a flag to reach the API: running `ddflow abandon <id> --discard` either forwards a keyword the lambda does not declare (because `L.merge_kwargs` is supplied as call kwargs) and raises `TypeError`, or silently ignores the flag if the framework filters it, leaving the worktree and branch in place. Either way the regression case for the explicit-discard path cannot pass, and the intended disposal after the flag never occurs. The same merge-kwargs reuse on `complete` applies merge options to a command whose lambda does not accept them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle.py:687,719 (abandon/remove CliPolicy; same pattern at complete :633)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion is `assert "worktree and branch removed" in out or "standing in it" in out`, but the two branches are not interchangeable for this setup. `_seed(repo, "T7")` claims the item and the test then invokes the CLI via `run_cli(repo, ...)`, i.e. the caller is at the repository root and is *not* standing in the worktree, so the only correct outcome for a clean tree is that the tree and branch are removed and that message is printed. Because the `or` accepts the "standing in it" message — the outcome for a completely different situation (caller inside the tree) that cannot legitimately arise here — a regression in the CLI's caller-cwd detection or in its disposition reporting (e.g. it keeps every tree and reports "standing in it") would still make this test pass. The test therefore does not guard the user-visible behavior it is named for; it should assert the removal message specifically (or assert absence of the keep message) for the not-in-tree caller.

chunk_findings.detail: The change is presented as the fix for bug B79319c6ada (abandon/remove must dispose the item's worktree and `ddflow/<id>` branch, keeping a tree with uncommitted files or unmerged commits unless `--discard` is given), and the intent states the regression test must exercise abandon and be watched to FAIL on the unfixed code. The only test file added here does not touch that path at all: every test calls `claim` / `release` / `LC.complete` / `brief` / `sweep_finished` and asserts on completed-item tree sweeping for the unrelated bug B4757c428f4 (see the module docstring). There is no call to the abandon path (`api/lifecycle/complete.abandon`) and no call to the remove path anywhere in the diff, and no assertion about the keep-the-tree-and-name-the-branch outcome or the `--discard` backup-ref behaviour that the intent describes. Concretely, running this suite against the unfixed code (where abandon/remove leave the tree and branch behind) still passes all seven tests, because none of them invoke abandon or remove — so it cannot serve as the "fails before the fix" regression test the intent requires, and the bug being closed has no regression coverage, contrary to the hard "must have regression test" constraint in [D-rules-hierarchy]. The tests also do not cover the "unmerged commits keep the tree" branch of the new behaviour, which is the dangerous case for any automatic tree/branch disposal.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_finished_tree_sweep.py

chunk_findings.detail: `brief` is the entry point for every session start, and it now unconditionally invokes `CL.sweep_finished`, whose stated criterion is only "DONE items finished long enough ago" (`worktree.dispose_finished` defaults to `true`, `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` to `3600`). That criterion is not the one the fix direction for this change mandates: disposal is only allowed for a *clean* tree with *no unmerged commits*, and "adopted and borrowed trees are never touched", with any kept tree reported by naming its branch and the command to inspect it. Nothing in the calling code enforces any of that, and the helper discards the call's result entirely (it returns `None`), so no kept/removed outcome is ever surfaced to the operator. Concretely: an item created with the default `worktree.adopt_existing = true` (a pre-existing directory the user adopted) that reaches DONE and is left alone for an hour is removed by the next `brief` run from *any* agent — including a `brief` issued from inside that very worktree by a session that is still using it (the process' CWD becomes a deleted directory, and its relative paths fail). The same happens to a DONE-but-not-yet-merged item whose only tree is clean but whose branch has unmerged commits, if the sweep's own cleanliness/merge check is missing or weaker than the one required for `abandon`/`remove`. Because `_sweep_finished` wraps the call in `except Exception: pass`, none of this is reported: if the sweep is wrong or only partially completes (tree gone, git metadata left behind), the operator sees no error and the doctor's orphan report quietly persists or changes shape. The unsafe part is the silent, default-on destructive side effect in a session-start read path with no operator-visible outcome; the testable input is "worktree adopted (or DONE with unmerged commits), age > `worktree.sweep_min_age_s`, then any `ddflow brief`".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/brief.py:170 `_sweep_finished`

chunk_findings.detail:
`remove` appends the node-deletion event *before* delegating to `_dispose`, and `_dispose` re-derives the item from a fresh fold:

```python
log.append("phase.removed" if it.kind == "phase" else "task.removed", item, {"reason": reason})
return O.ok("item.removed", ..., **_dispose(repo, cfg, log, item, (called_from, shell_cwd)))
...
it = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False).items.get(item)
removed, why = CL.dispose_finished(repo, cfg, log, it, callers=callers) if it is not None else (False, "")
```

The removal event is deliberately node-scoped (`task.removed` / `phase.removed` — "Take an item out of the queue entirely"), unlike `item.abandoned`, which is a state transition that keeps the node. Once that event is in the log, the re-fold no longer yields the item, so `it is None`, the `if it is not None` guard short-circuits, and `dispose_finished` is never invoked for `remove`. Concretely: `ddflow remove <id>` on an item with a clean merged worktree leaves `[REDACTED:path]<id>` and `ddflow/<id>` in place exactly as before the fix, and the outcome it prints is `worktree_removed: false` with `kept_reason: ""` — i.e. no disposal and no explanation, so the operator cannot even tell that the tree was kept. This is the same bug B79319c6ada for the `remove` half; because `_dispose` swallows the missing-item case as `(False, "")` instead of an error or the real reason, it also cannot be noticed from the output. (The stated regression tests only cover `abandon`, which is why this path is not caught.) Moving the `_dispose` call above the terminal `log.append`, or passing the already-folded `it` in, would fix the ordering.

chunk_findings.detail: `dispose_finished` only protects a live shell via the explicit `callers` tuple (`stands_in(path, *callers)`), and `sweep_finished` invokes it as `dispose_finished(repo, cfg, log, it)` with the default `callers=()`. `stands_in` then iterates over an empty sequence and always returns `False`, so the guard that exists precisely to avoid "the next `pwd` fails" (B1172da8c35, quoted in the new `stands_in` docstring) is inert on the session-start sweep. Given a DONE item whose tree was kept at merge time because its caller stood in it, a shell that stays in that worktree past `worktree.sweep_min_age_s` and then runs the session-start sweep gets its cwd deleted: the age gate only proves the item finished long ago, not that anyone left the directory. `sweep_finished` should pass the process'/client's cwd the same way the `merge` path does.

data.claim: The queue has no task for the gaps below; most of the surface is already planned (ACP, spawn, caps, governor, platform MCP, control planes); the real gaps are a Codex app-server lane backend with dynamic tools, native subagent definition sync and native cap mapping, a table fan-out run, a Symphony-style tracker contract, a work receipt, a human-review capacity cap, a per-worktree bootstrap, and an agent roster with scorecards.
data.falsifier: A probe of the installed Codex shows the app-server lacks thread/turn/approval methods or dynamic tools, or the .codex/agents TOML cannot carry what the sync needs; then FL-codex-appserver and FL-subagent-sync shrink to the exec and MCP routes.
data.mechanism: CODEX: subagents are TOML files in [REDACTED:path] or .codex/agents (name, description, developer_instructions; optional model, reasoning effort/summary, verbosity); built-ins default, worker, explorer; limits agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session (default 6), max_depth (default 1); subagents inherit the parent sandbox and approvals and cannot override them; results are consolidated by the parent; /subagents switches threads; spawn_agents_on_csv fans one worker out per CSV row; codex exec --json streams events headlessly; codex mcp-server exposes codex and codex-reply; the app-server is a JSON-RPC headless mode. SYMPHONY (OpenAI, 2026-04-28, Apache-2.0): a tracker board (Linear) as control plane over the Codex app-server; one isolated workspace per ticket, restarts crashed runs, posts proof of work (CI status, PR feedback, complexity) back to the ticket; dynamic tool calls instead of MCP so no token enters the container; a SPEC reimplemented per language. FRONTIER (2026-02-05): an enterprise platform to build, deploy and manage agents: shared business context, an execution environment, evaluation and optimization, agent identity with scoped permissions and governance; open to agents built elsewhere. PITFALLS named by practitioners: token cost grows with every agent, human review is the bottleneck (3-5 agents is the sweet spot), isolation does not give dependency alignment, depth above 1 explodes cost. ALREADY PLANNED IN DDFLOW (reused, not redone): P-acp (client, wrap, thin agent, permissions, steering, resume), P-spawn (route, steer, notify, tree, context), P-agent-caps (group caps, slots), P-governor (tiers, step cost, regret), P-platform-mcp (PM-codex-mcp, search-and-call facade), P-control-planes (intake, exporters, notify sinks, env ports), P-safeguards (envelopes, dispatch brief), P-knowledge-hub (shared context), P-observe (feedback proposals). GAPS: no Codex app-server backend or dynamic-tool door; no sync of ddflow subagent definitions with .codex/agents TOML and no mapping of ddflow caps onto Codex's own thread and depth limits; no table fan-out run; no tracker contract Symphony could drive; no work receipt posted to the ticket; review capacity is capped only for autopilot proposals; no per-worktree dependency bootstrap; no agent roster with identity, scopes and scorecards.

data.mechanism: GRAPH: 909 open tasks in 78 phases, no cycles, no priority inversions, 0 dangling needs (needs on abandoned decide tasks are settled decisions). Depth 20 (CN-acceptance). 880 of ~890 non-running tasks are blocked behind two hubs, B-gap-log-scale (43 direct dependents) and B-gap-plan-lint (42); B-gap-log-scale needs the unphased B-log-snapshot-knobs. 355 needs edges are transitively redundant. 22 open tasks have no phase (B-semantic-recall, B-mcp-http-transport, fix-test-duration-*, ...) and cannot be moved until P-reshape.move exists. HOT FILES: README.md is listed by 63 open tasks (47 not docs tasks), ddflow/config.py by 58 (57 not), ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py by 56 (47 not), core/events.py 32, api/lifecycle 31; 93 percent of the pairs are unordered, so the conflict detector will serialise them at run time. D-readme-split, SE-globs and P-change-surface exist to fix this but the old phases still carry the coarse globs. DUPLICATES: the open-only near-duplicate pairs are template twins, not copies: the per-phase -docs (0.7-0.9), -surfaces (0.7), -eval and -acceptance tasks repeat one shape in 16 phases and each says 'table generated from the descriptors'; the P-change-surface.split-* tasks are mechanical twins. They share the declared-commands, docs-generation and SE-eval-harness engines; the risk is each phase writing its own table generator. DECISIONS: 164 records, 138 live, 23 superseded (chains sound), 3 proposed (D-B191-item-ids, D-gate-ratio-noise, D-old-work-behind-core-docs). 620 of 909 open tasks cite or inherit a specific decision; 289 do not (P-test-domains, P-docs-generic, P-subagents, P-agent-memory, P-observe, P-test-robustness, P-pipeline-ideas, P-agent-rules, P-resume, P-spawn, P-lessons, P-context-sync, P-reasoning, P-doc-templates and others) although same-named decisions exist for several (D-observe, D-subagents, D-perf, D-remote, D-agent-caps, D-agent-parity, D-agent-lifecycle, D-extension-seams, D-reasoning-log, D-session-context); P-spawn, P-resume, P-test-robustness, P-lessons, P-agent-hygiene, P-change-surface have no decision of their own. There is no structural task-to-decision link, only globs and prose. CONTRADICTIONS AND OVERLAPS: (1) D-subagents lets a declared other-family subagent count as a reviewer with no approval and says itself that it relaxes D-reviewer-trust; B-sub-trust is kept; the base rule was never amended. (2) D-upgrade-auto-check says auto=check never writes, D-upgrade-on-mcp-connect starts the upgrade on a version difference, D-self-upgrade-defaults applies safe categories at container start. (3) D-sched-no-daemon says no daemon; D-remote refines it; D-knowledge-hub adds an HTTP hub; the base text was not amended. (4) Ordering is spread over D-pause-after-upgrade, D-order-cleanup-then-upgrade-features, D-phase-order-gaps-first, D-phase-order-core-records-first, D-old-work-note-r1, D-schedule-early, D-perf-core-wave, all amending the still-PROPOSED D-old-work-behind-core-docs. (5) D-readme-current (every change updates the README) against D-readme-split (README is a front door): 63 tasks still name README.md. (6) D-push-after-acceptance still says nothing is pushed until P-unify acceptance passes although P-unify is done. (7) Agent authority is spread over D-stack-tools (agent accepts any tool role), D-decision-management, D-export-agent-enable, D-doc-types, D-product-docs-r3, D-safeguards, D-subagents, D-reviewer-trust, D-autopilot with no single matrix. MERGE CANDIDATES: the four export decisions; the upgrade family (about 12); the four enum-fallback decisions (D-enum-fallback-strict, D-fallback-no-remote, D6fc09b2590, D9b8061fd38); the three skills decisions; D-perf with D-no-duckdb; the MCP-surface decisions (D-lean-and-trusted, D-tools-list-budget-100k, D-mcp-output-schemas-off, D-viewer-lists-consolidated); D-quotas with D-governor. ENGINE OVERLAPS CHECKED AND SOUND: meters (B-quota-meters is the root; P-agent-parity.meters, P-governor.context-meter, PM-meters follow it), descriptors (P-agent-parity.descriptor-v2 is the root of 18), approvals (SE-ask-core), notifications (P-spawn.notify to CP-notify-sinks to CP-attention). data.decision: Operator 2026-10-14 (AskUserQuestion, RH-decide). (1) REVIEWER RULE: operator-authored subagent definitions with an explicit other-family model id count as an independent reviewer with no approval; agent-authored or tool-widening definitions need operator approval by digest (B-sub-trust); D-reviewer-trust is amended to point here. (2) UPGRADE: session start only prints the one-line notice ([upgrade].auto=check); on MCP connect the agent proposes the upgrade and the operator consents; container start applies safe categories only, and only when [upgrade].auto is safe. (3) DAEMONS, verbatim: 'I want to explore the option of ddflow to be able to start daemon if it decides, in addition to the operator, with notification to the operator, unless this is forbidden by config, or policy, and ddflow to be able manage the daemon life stages, start, stop, monitor, attach, disconnect, etc - whatever is expected'. Followed by the answer to the policy question (Allowed by default for a declared list; notify, the recommended option): config lists the daemon kinds ddflow may start itself; each start is logged and shown in brief and notification sinks; config, policy or [daemon].auto=off forbids it; a kind not on the list needs the operator. D-sched-no-daemon is therefore to be AMENDED after the research P-daemon (DM-research), not yet superseded; until then no daemon starts. (4) ORDER: one current roadmap-order decision replaces the seven ordering notes and the three proposed decisions (D-old-work-behind-core-docs, D-B191-item-ids, D-gate-ratio-noise) are accepted as they stand; done by RH-merge-decisions (superseding records, nothing deleted). (5) README: front door only; each task updates its docs fragment, generated tables included; D-readme-current is superseded by this record and RH-hot-globs rewrites the task globs. (6) PUSH: see D-push-operator-says. (7) ORDER OF ENGINES: SE-actors and SE-ask-core move ahead to priority 11, and B-dt-drafts needs SE-ask-core. (8) MERGES: pure-merge consolidations (export 4, enum fallback 4, skills 3, perf with no-duckdb, MCP surface 4) may be made as superseding records without asking per group; anything that changes meaning comes back as a question. (9) NEW AREAS: all three are to be built: the dependency guard (AG-deps-guard), OpenTelemetry export and ingest (AG-otel), and A2A (AG-a2a), at their queued priorities.

Candidates: scheduler tick, serve on loopback, knowledge-hub mirror, file and upstream watchers, the resident MCP state, lane supervisors. data.claim: Yes: the storage seam, writer ratchet, lock strategy, merge strategy and locality split are one staged line that reuses P-remote.serve, the declared-command matrix and the org-config layer stack; B-mcp-http-transport duplicates P-remote.serve and must fold into it; B110 is mostly done already.

data.mechanism: ORIGINAL REQUEST (operator 2026-09-25, recorded in R14 and B109-B112): four parts: can a user ask what the workflow is and change it per project (answered: ddflow_workflow and friends); could the config live in a file the AGENT reads and writes on the server's behalf; could the other stores work the same way so the server needs no filesystem; and how is persistence implemented. THE IDEA: run the MCP server remotely or in a container without direct filesystem access. R14 REFUTED delegating file I/O to the agent over MCP (no primitive: roots/list is file:// URIs, sampling, elicitation; re-checked against the 2026-07-28 spec) and found that git, not storage, is the real coupling: concurrent-branch safety is merge=union on the event shards, flock is POSIX-only, gates run shell=True in a local worktree. The honest shape: a REMOTE-CAPABLE half (the queue as data) and a LOCAL-REQUIRED half (worktrees, merge, tree-fingerprint evidence, command gates). B109 storage seam (no abstraction exists), B110 scattered writers, B111 git coupling (THEORETICAL), B112 the split (build deliberately or not at all), plus B13 Windows (flock). WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE: (1) infra/fsio.py with atomic_write now exists and 12 modules use it, so B110's premise is mostly met (a search of its seven modules finds one raw write, gates/mutation.py); (2) D-remote (2026-10-12) chose an opt-in, stateless ddflow serve with state staying in the log, and P-remote.serve/auth/events/runs/ask implement the remote-capable half over the declared commands; (3) B-mcp-http-transport (operator 2026-09-29) asks for the same HTTP MCP server as P-remote.serve (TWO queue items for ONE server); (4) P-change-surface.split-log-records will turn infra/log.py (84 KB), core/records.py and infra/store.py into packages, so any seam must land after it or it is rewritten twice; (5) B-gap-log-scale moves gate evidence out of line (services/logblobs.py), a blob store that belongs behind the same seam; (6) P-knowledge-hub plans a reference hub whose storage is append-only with sequence (KB-hub) and a local SQLite mirror (KB-mirror), P-constellation a read-only sibling mirror, P-daemon a managed serve and hub mirror: each would otherwise invent its own storage; (7) P-core-records.matrix (running) builds a verb x kind x surface matrix, the natural home for a LOCALITY column (remote-capable or local-required); (8) P-org-config has a layer stack the client-held config of the original question can join as a session layer; (9) B13 now spans infra/fsio.py and services/flowstate.py as well as log.py and tomlcfg.py. COLLISIONS FOUND: B109 and B13 have identical globs; both and P-change-surface.split-log-records rewrite infra/log.py; B110 lists the whole services/gates/ directory against fix-gate-python-version (a lock clash, its real target is one file); B-mcp-http-transport and P-remote.serve both write surfaces/mcp.py or its serve replacement. MERGE PLAN: keep all four ideas and B13 as the real implementation items, re-scoped and ordered, and add a small phase P-storage with the decision, the writer ratchet, the locality tag, the merge-strategy interface, the client config overlay, and an acceptance with no filesystem on the client side.

- **B109. A storage seam behind `EventLog` and `tomlcfg`. FILED.** There is no storage
  abstraction of any kind today (`grep` for `Protocol|ABC|abstractmethod|Backend` across

  events, `infra/tomlcfg.py` for TOML — and most services already go through them.
  Introducing a backend interface there, with the filesystem as the default

data.body:
- **B111. The git coupling is the real blocker, and it is not storage. FILED,
  THEORETICAL.** `cli.py:216` writes `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl merge=union` into
  `.gitattributes`, so **concurrent-branch safety is delegated to git's own union merge
  driver**: two agents on two branches append to their own shards and git unions them
  with no conflict. That is the conflict-resolution strategy, not an implementation
  detail, and it exists only because the log is a file in the repo. On top of it:
  `fcntl.flock` is POSIX single-machine (`log.py:197`, `tomlcfg.py:114`); gate and
  reviewer commands run `shell=True` against a local worktree (`gates.py:776`,
  `review.py:485`, `review.py:782`); every git call is `git -C <local-path>`. A remote
  backend would have to REPLACE the merge strategy, not just the storage — and would
  still leave worktrees, merge and tree-fingerprint evidence needing the real checkout.

Imported from docs/BACKLOG.md:1429.

RE-SCOPED 2026-10-15 (R-storage-seam, phase P-storage; the original text above is kept): The git coupling stays the honest constraint. It becomes a tested design: ST-merge-strategy defines the interface (git-union default, serve-sequenced append for the remote mode) and proves both fold the same events; close this item when that test shows what each strategy can and cannot do. Remote is serve as the single writer (D-remote), not a replacement of git for local branches.

Operator 2026-09-29, from a fact-check of 'works with remote agents': today the MCP server is stdio only (surfaces/mcp.py), so a remote agent needs its own clone and shares state through git. Add `ddflow mcp --http HOST:PORT` implementing MCP streamable HTTP over the same TOOLS registry (no second implementation). Security first: bind [REDACTED:ipv4] by default; refuse a non-loopback bind without a bearer token (token from an env var or a machine-local file, never config); per-connection identity (a remote client must declare it, as ddflow_identify does); one repo per server. The sequential-request assumption behind the unlocked parse cache (infra/log.py _PARSE_CACHE) must hold or be guarded — serialize tool calls per server. Tests: a real HTTP round-trip of initialize/tools/list/tools/call; refusal without a token on 0.0.0.0; two clients get distinct identities.

R-agent-compat (2026-10-08). Needed by B-ac-bot-model: cloud agents that accept only remote MCP servers (Devin, Cursor cloud agents, Copilot with OAuth-less remote servers) need this transport; coordinate its tests with B-ac-mcp-tests.

Audit 2026-10-10: decide and record whether the streamable-HTTP transport is stdlib or uses the optional [mcp-sdk] extra (D-unify 2: official SDK only for the HTTP transport); if stdlib, ask the operator to remove the unused mcp-sdk extra and update its pyproject.toml comment. Add the [mcp-sdk] doctor line either way (see B-arch-unify-leftovers (b)).

RE-SCOPED 2026-10-15 (R-storage-seam, phase P-storage; the original text above is kept): FOLDED into P-remote.serve (one stateless server, one authorization table over the declared commands, streamable HTTP MCP plus the JSON /v1 API; D-remote). Do not write a second transport: this item keeps only what serve does not already specify (the operator's 2026-09-29 security rules: loopback default, bearer token required for a non-loopback bind, token from an environment variable or machine-local file never config, per-connection identity) as acceptance tests against serve, plus the alias ddflow mcp --http HOST:PORT. (1) REMOTE QUEUE: yes, staged after the log package split: writer ratchet (ST-writers), P-change-surface.split-log-records, the storage seam (B109), the locality column (ST-locality, B112), the merge-strategy interface (ST-merge-strategy, B111), then the acceptance (ST-acceptance). (3) CONFIG OVERLAY: yes, a session layer: the client sends an overlay with the session; it ranks above project config and below operator-only keys, is logged with its digest, expires with the session, never widens operator-only settings and never carries the event log (ST-config-overlay). (4) WINDOWS: probe first (a Windows CI leg or probe before any support claim; B13 closes as won't-do if it fails). (5) MEMORY BACKEND: yes, built with the seam for test isolation. All as recommended.

data.body:
Per D-storage (operator 2026-10-15): worktrees, merge, tree-fingerprint evidence, command gates and hooks are local-required (ST-locality). A remote client is refused with the local alternative UNLESS the operator enabled a paired local executor: a small local process, paired with a scoped token (CP-scoped-tokens), that runs exactly the commands the served queue hands it, inside the lease globs of the item, in the item's worktree, and returns the result as the gate or merge outcome. Reuses the lane backend interface (CP-backend-iface: start, report, stop, status), the approvals engine for the first pairing and any command outside an allowlist (SE-ask-core), and the daemon life cycle (DM-lifecycle, a listed lane-supervisor kind: operator-only per D-daemons). Off by default; pairing, allowlist, timeouts and output caps are [executor] knobs; every dispatch, result and refusal is a logged event; a result is evidence only when the executor identity matches the paired token. Seeded faults: an executor asked for a command outside its allowlist, a replayed dispatch, an executor that returns a pass without running, a stale pairing.
